title: Three Countries on One River: Real or Not?

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *que* + subjunctive for something unknown or non-existent from B2 Unit 13: if the thing is real and you can point at it, *que* takes the indicative; if you are only looking for it, or it does not exist, it takes the subjunctive. At the point where Colombia, Brazil and Peru meet, the border works in surprising ways. Here the pattern works on Leticia and Tabatinga.

sections.title: Real, or only wanted?
rows: Leticia y Tabatinga son dos ciudades que forman una zona continua.
No hay ninguna valla que separe las dos ciudades.
Un viajero busca un lugar donde se hablen español y portugués.
En el mercado hay personas que hablan los dos idiomas.

items.spanish: Hay una isla que pertenece a Perú.
items.english: There is an island that belongs to Peru.

items.spanish: No hay ningún puente que una las dos orillas en ese punto.
items.english: There is no bridge that joins the two banks at that point.

items.spanish: Necesitamos una escuela que enseñe en los dos idiomas.
items.english: We need a school that teaches in both languages.

sections.content: Ask one question: can I point at it? If yes, indicative. If it is only wanted, needed or imagined, or if you say it does not exist (*no hay ninguna ... que*), use the subjunctive. Keep the personal *a* before a person: *Busco a alguien que ...*.
